forces: Mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: Live, 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg
question: How can a movement remain urgent while changing the way the choir speaks?
intro: The Sequence begins with a compact choral outburst: restless strings, forceful syllables and little room to recover between phrases. Within that pressure, Mozart distinguishes collective proclamation from a later exchange between the choral basses and the upper voices. The traditional completion supplies instrumental detail beyond Mozart’s surviving draft.

sections.label: A · Collective warning
sections.mNote: Block declamation and moving lines share the same restless accompaniment

sections.label: B · Divided voices
sections.mNote: Repeated choral bass notes alternate with broader upper voices

sections.label: C · Final drive
sections.mNote: The choir gathers before a short orchestral conclusion

cues.title: Syllables over a rushing surface
cues.text: The choir’s opening words strike in blocks while the strings move in much smaller notes. Listen to those two speeds at once: the singers give the text weight, but the accompaniment prevents the chords from becoming stationary.
cues.evidence: Mutopia’s public-domain engraving, based on Breitkopf 1877, opening bars; NMA p. 62. The report shows an immediate high-level span after the file begins. This describes the opening texture without assigning instrumental attacks to exact seconds.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A text about judgement
cues.text: Dies irae means “day of wrath”. These opening verses of the Requiem Sequence picture judgement and trembling. Mozart sets the Latin text here; the movement’s identity should not be confused with a quotation of the familiar plainchant melody.
cues.evidence: The score prints the Sequence text and Mozart’s own choral setting: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/cgibin/piece-info.cgi?id=364. This note concerns the movement as a whole, not the word sung at 0:18.

cues.title: The warning renews its force
cues.text: The early passage repeatedly rebuilds its force after small withdrawals. Follow the fast string motion through those changes: continuity in the accompaniment binds together the choir’s more sharply articulated phrases.
cues.evidence: The report places a local retreat around 0:30 between stronger windows at 0:15–0:20 and 0:35. The continuous smaller-note string writing comes from the score, not an instrument separator.

cues.title: A concert after a symphony
cues.text: The source is a live Salzburg Festival concert, not a recording of a funeral service. The Vienna Philharmonic’s archive pairs the Requiem with Mozart’s Symphony No. 25 and dates the event to 26 July 1956.
cues.evidence: Primary concert listing: https://www.wienerphilharmoniker.at/en/konzerte/salzburg-festival/512/. Internet Archive item MozartRequiemBruno identifies the live recording. Session, release and upload dates are kept separate in the dossier.

cues.title: The basses change the argument
cues.text: In the contrasting later stretch, the choral basses press repeated notes while the upper voices answer in broader rhythms. Listen for the exchange between registers. This is the choir’s bass section, not a new solo for the bass singer.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 71–73 and Mutopia pp. 6–7 show the choral-bass Quantus tremor figures alternating with upper-voice Dies irae. The report’s 1:02 boundary and lower 1:05–1:15 span locate this contrast approximately; no sung phrase is precisely aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The orchestra has the last word
cues.text: The final vocal statements gather the choir again, but the singers do not sustain the final bars. The strings carry a brief, still restless conclusion after the last choral syllable. Listen for motion continuing after the text has stopped.
cues.evidence: NMA pp. 76–77: the choir finishes in bar 65 and rests through the orchestral close in bars 66–68. The report remains active through 1:45, then falls sharply by 1:50. These are passage limits, not a timed claim for the last syllable.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A repeated bass figure divides the choir
transitions.how: The continuous fast accompaniment survives, but the choir’s organisation changes. Choral basses repeat a narrow figure on the words about trembling, while the upper voices answer with broader rhythms. A low repeated pitch focuses the tension without bringing a new tempo. The contrast is made inside the same ensemble: register, syllabic repetition and the spacing of the entries replace another undifferentiated tutti.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 71–73; Mutopia pp. 6–7. The report’s 1:02 boundary and lower level around 1:05–1:15 provisionally anchor the passage. Repeated notes are read from the score, not inferred from machine bass estimates.

transitions.title: The separate calls gather into a conclusion
transitions.how: The alternating registers give way to renewed collective weight. The strings retain their rushing subdivisions while the choir presses the final judgement text towards a cadence. Repeated statements consolidate D minor rather than opening a contrasting lyrical section. After the singers finish, the orchestra completes the movement with a short continuation of the same restless motion.
transitions.evidence: NMA pp. 74–77; Mutopia pp. 7–9. The report’s 1:20 boundary is followed by higher relative level at 1:20–1:25 and 1:35. This supports the final drive, not a specific chord at 1:20.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr, Dies irae, Martin Norbäck engraving after Breitkopf 1877
source.locator: Public-domain engraving, pp. 1–9; checked against NMA pp. 62–77. Broad passage states, not bar-aligned entrances or continuous activity. Basset horns lack a stage token. Trombones are withheld because the older edition and Walter’s reported cuts do not establish a session-specific doubling map.

timeline.note: Forceful choral declamation sits above rapid strings; brass and timpani punctuate the opening rather than carrying its melody.
The contrast is inside the choir: repeated bass figures and broader upper-voice answers. Trumpets and timpani contribute only brief punctuation.
The final choral drive regains collective weight while the rapid orchestral surface continues.
In the short scored postlude the choir is silent; the orchestra completes the cadence. This boundary is approximate.
The report drops to the file’s low final tail; no new scored activity is assigned.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Traditional Mozart–Süssmayr completion, Dies irae; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
fields.note: Mozart left the vocal and bass framework and some instrumental indications; the traditional completed orchestration is used as the reference. The recording sources do not name a printed edition. The NMA preface quotes Walter’s policy of cutting some trombone doublings, but does not map it to this 1956 performance. The complete movement includes its orchestral postlude.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
fields.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: No catalogue number is attached to the transferred source. Cetra LO516, Nuova Era 2209, Seven Seas K30Y307 and Orfeo C430961B are documented release leads only. The festival catalogue dates Orfeo C 430 961 B to 1996; that is not evidence of first release or byte provenance.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied for the source used. The file is a complete movement from a live performance; neither a shellac carrier nor an original tape generation is established. No physical side join is assigned to a musical event.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: D. Benjamin Miller is the Commons uploader, not an established transfer or mastering engineer. The Internet Archive uploader/scanner fields document repository submission, not who digitised, edited or restored the recording. No transfer-engineer credit has been found.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Internet Archive added/public date is 4 June 2018; Commons upload is 5 June 2018. These are not transfer dates. The embedded Commons digitizing year 1956 duplicates the performance year without a transfer history and is not accepted as such evidence. The 1996 Orfeo issue is also not assigned as the date of this transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Internet Archive lists the corresponding Ogg Vorbis movement file as an original upload; Commons supplies Ogg Vorbis and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: Here original means the repository’s uploaded file, not an original session master. The chain from the unidentified physical or broadcast source to the Ogg is undocumented. Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
fields.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue
K. or KV = Ludwig von Köchel’s catalogue, first published in 1862 and repeatedly revised
composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.
